Purpose To investigate the effects of different recovery strategies on fatigue markers following a prolonged running exercise. Methods 46 recreational male runners completed a half-marathon, followed by active recovery (ACT), cold water immersion (CWI), massage (MAS) or passive recovery (PAS). Countermovement jump height, muscle soreness and perceived recovery and stress were measured 24h before the half-marathon (pre), immediately after the recovery intervention (post rec ) and 24h after the race (post 24 ). In addition, muscle contractile properties and blood markers of fatigue were determined at pre and post 24 . Results Magnitude-based inferences revealed substantial differences in the changes between the groups. At post rec , ACT was harmful to perceived recovery (ACT vs. PAS: effect size [ES] = −1.81) and serum concentration of creatine kinase (ACT vs. PAS: ES = 0.42), with CWI being harmful to jump performance (CWI vs. PAS: ES = −0.98). It was also beneficial for reducing muscle soreness (CWI vs. PAS: ES = −0.88) and improving perceived stress (CWI vs. PAS: ES = −0.64), with MAS being beneficial for reducing muscle soreness (MAS vs. PAS: ES = −0.52) and improving perceived recovery (MAS vs. PAS: ES = 1.00). At post 24 , both CWI and MAS were still beneficial for reducing muscle soreness (CWI vs. PAS: ES = 1.49; MAS vs. PAS: ES = 1.12), with ACT being harmful to perceived recovery (ACT vs. PAS: ES = −0.68), serum concentration of creatine kinase (ACT vs. PAS: ES = 0.84) and free-testosterone (ACT vs. PAS: ES = −0.91). Conclusions In recreational runners, a half-marathon results in fatigue symptoms lasting at least 24h. To restore subjective fatigue measures, the authors recommend CWI and MAS, as these recovery strategies are more effective than PAS, with ACT being even disadvantageous. Introduction A long-distance running exercise such as a half-marathon or a marathon is one of the most strenuous activities because it combines a prolonged duration with an eccentric component and a relatively high exercise intensity [ 1 ]. Although the resultant post-exercise fatigue is based on many factors (e.g. related to the central nervous system and/or peripheral factors within the skeletal muscles) that have not yet been fully explored because of their complexity, it is usually reflected in a substantial decrease in muscle performance that can last up to several days [ 2 , 3 ]. Thus, the use of recovery strategies seems to be required to overcome the demands of, for example, a half-marathon- or a marathon-type exertion, to increase the athlete’s well-being and allow them to return to normal training as quickly as possible without increased risk of injury or illness [ 4 , 5 ]. A variety of recovery methods can help to alleviate the deleterious effects of muscle fatigue caused by strenuous exercise [ 6 ]. Apart from nutritional strategies, three of the best known recovery interventions are active recovery (also referred to as active cool-down and usually consisting of aerobic-type whole-body activities, such as running, biking or swimming) [ 7 ], cold water immersion [ 8 ] and massage [ 9 ]. Although numerous studies have investigated their efficacy, most have used non-functional exercises to induce fatigue. Unfortunately, there are limited studies investigating the potential effectiveness of recovery strategies in road running. However, post-exercise fatigue varies in type and degree depending on the characteristics of the exercise that brings on the fatigue [ 2 ]. Therefore, the findings of the majority of these studies may not apply to the actual practice of long-distance runners. Only one previous study investigated the effect of cold water immersion on the markers of recovery following a marathon. Wilson et al. [ 10 ] showed that cold water immersion is no more effective than a placebo effect in improving functional recovery or perceptions of muscle soreness and exercise stress following a road race. Similarly, Dawson et al. [ 11 ] observed no effect of massage applied after a half-marathon road race on the recovery of muscles, either in terms of physiological measures of strength and swelling or perceived muscle pain. Sherman et al. [ 12 ] compared the effect of running at low intensities (i.e. active recovery) with that of passive recovery over one week following a marathon. Their findings showed that active recovery did not facilitate the restoration of marathon-induced reductions in muscle function. In summary, although the incorporation of recovery strategies into a period of regeneration is becoming increasingly popular across both recreational and elite level runners, the aforementioned studies unanimously report that recovery interventions do not promote recovery from marathon-induced fatigue. However, because of the small number of studies that have examined the use of recovery methods in long-distance running, little evidence seems to support the efficacy or inefficacy of active recovery, cold water immersion, or massage in recovery following a marathon-type exertion. Moreover, to our knowledge, no study has yet compared the effects of various recovery strategies following road running within a single-study setting. Therefore, this study aimed to compare the effects of active recovery, cold water immersion, massage and passive recovery on fatigue markers in recreational runners following the completion of a half-marathon run.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of various post-exercise recovery strategies (active recovery, cold water immersion, massage, and passive recovery) on subjective and objective fatigue markers in 46 recreational male runners after a competitive half-marathon. The findings indicate that cold water immersion and massage were effective in improving subjective fatigue measures, such as muscle soreness and perceived recovery/stress, compared to passive recovery. However, active recovery was largely ineffective or even detrimental, worsening subjective recovery and negatively impacting certain objective markers (creatine kinase, free-testosterone). Overall, none of the recovery interventions demonstrated beneficial effects on objective physiological markers of fatigue.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Post-exercise recovery interventions (Active Recovery (ACT), Cold Water Immersion (CWI), Massage (MAS), and Passive Recovery (PAS)) following a half-marathon race.
treatment_details.dose_specificity:
46 recreational male runners completed a competitive half-marathon (average time 107-116 min, 86.2%-92.9% of anaerobic threshold, 450 m altitude climb). Within 15 minutes post-race, a single application of one of four recovery protocols was performed: Passive Recovery (PAS) was 15 min sitting at rest; Active Recovery (ACT) was 15 min sub-maximal jogging at 60% anaerobic threshold; Cold Water Immersion (CWI) involved 15 min of lower limb immersion up to the iliac crest in 15 
	1
	C water, with circular leg motions every 2 min; and Massage (MAS) consisted of 20 min of classical sports massage (effleurage, petrissage, friction), split into 5 min per leg in prone and supine positions, performed by certified sports scientists. No dose-response comparisons for the overall half-marathon intensity or the recovery interventions were explicitly reported, though the CWI protocol was chosen based on existing dose-response evidence.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: The half-marathon itself increased CK levels. Active recovery (ACT) significantly increased CK levels compared to passive recovery (PAS) immediately post-recovery (ES = 0.42) and at 24 hours post-race (ES = 0.84), indicating a harmful effect. Cold water immersion (CWI) and massage (MAS) showed no beneficial effect on CK levels.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An enzyme released from muscle cells into the bloodstream, serving as a primary indicator of muscle damage and metabolic stress.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a half-marathon race and various recovery strategies (active, cold water immersion, massage, or passive).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the level of muscle damage and breakdown; higher levels suggest increased muscle soreness, reduced performance, and impaired physiological muscle recovery, particularly exacerbated by active recovery.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Active recovery (ACT) resulted in substantially lower free-testosterone levels at 24 hours post-race compared to passive recovery (PAS) (ES = -0.91), indicating a harmful effect on hormonal balance. Other recovery strategies (CWI, MAS) showed no beneficial effect on free-testosterone levels.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A steroid hormone vital for anabolic processes, muscle repair, and recovery, also involved in neurohumoral regulation and muscle protein synthesis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a half-marathon race, especially after active recovery, measured 24 hours post-race.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates hormonal balance, anabolic capacity, and recovery status; lower levels reflect heightened physiological stress or impeded recovery, suggesting a less favorable anabolic environment.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: The half-marathon itself increased CRP levels. None of the recovery strategies (ACT, CWI, MAS) had a beneficial effect on CRP levels, which remained unchanged by these interventions acutely or at 24 hours post-race.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An acute phase reactant, serving as a general indicator of inflammation and stress.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a half-marathon race and various recovery strategies (active, cold water immersion, massage, or passive).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the level of physiological inflammation; an unchanged level suggests ineffectiveness of recovery strategies in mitigating post-exercise inflammatory response.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: The half-marathon itself increased urea levels. Active recovery (ACT) had no acute or medium-term effect on urea levels. No specific quantitative data provided for other recovery strategies.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An indicator of protein catabolism and overall metabolic stress.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a half-marathon race, specifically after active recovery.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates metabolic status; an unchanged level suggests ineffectiveness of active recovery in improving post-exercise metabolic recovery.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: The half-marathon itself altered IGF-1 levels. Massage (MAS) resulted in slightly lower IGF-1 levels at 24 hours post-race compared to passive recovery (PAS) (ES = -0.34), suggesting a small harmful effect. No beneficial effects were observed for active recovery (ACT) or cold water immersion (CWI).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A growth factor that mediates cell growth, anabolism, tissue repair, and muscle regeneration, and is involved in metabolic and neurohumoral regulation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a half-marathon race, particularly after massage, and generally after other recovery strategies.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates anabolic potential and tissue repair processes; lower levels suggest suppressed growth and recovery mechanisms or impaired physiological recovery.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Cold water immersion (CWI) resulted in lower CMJ performance immediately post-recovery compared to passive recovery (PAS) (ES = -0.98), indicating a harmful effect. Measurements were taken 24 h before, immediately after recovery, and 24 h after the race.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An indicator of lower body power, explosive strength, and overall neuromuscular function.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a half-marathon race, specifically after cold water immersion.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects the recovery of athletic performance capacity and neuromuscular function; lower height indicates reduced power and potentially inadequate recovery.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Both cold water immersion (CWI) and massage (MAS) significantly reduced muscle soreness compared to passive recovery (PAS). CWI lowered soreness immediately post-recovery (ES = -0.88) and at 24 hours (ES = -1.49). MAS also lowered soreness immediately post-recovery (ES = -0.52) and at 24 hours (ES = -1.12). Measured using a 100 mm Visual Analogue Scale.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Subjective perception of muscle pain and discomfort, commonly associated with delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a half-marathon race, specifically after cold water immersion and massage interventions.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the level of muscle discomfort and pain, a key symptom of delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), which can impair performance and perceived recovery.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Subjective perception rating (SRSS / category ratio scale)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Active recovery (ACT) significantly lowered perceived recovery immediately post-recovery (ES = -1.81) and at 24 hours (ES = -0.68), indicating a harmful effect. Massage (MAS) significantly improved perceived recovery immediately post-recovery (ES = 1.00). Measured using the Short Recovery and Stress Scale (SRSS).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Subjective assessment of overall recovery status, well-being, and physiological state.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a half-marathon race, specifically after active recovery and massage interventions.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the subjective sense of restoration and readiness for future activity; lower values suggest poorer recovery and can reflect increased fatigue.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Cold water immersion (CWI) significantly lowered perceived stress immediately post-recovery compared to passive recovery (PAS) (ES = -0.64), indicating a beneficial effect. Measured using the Short Recovery and Stress Scale (SRSS).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Subjective assessment of psychological burden and physiological stress perception.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a half-marathon race, specifically after cold water immersion.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates psychological recovery and overall well-being; lower levels suggest reduced psychological stress and improved recovery.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Maximal radial deformation (Dm) of the muscle belly

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Massage (MAS) resulted in slightly higher maximal radial deformation (Dm) at 24 hours post-race compared to passive recovery (PAS) (ES = 0.42), suggesting a small harmful effect, though its significance is cautioned by a high coefficient of variation (CV = 12.9%). Measured by Tensiomyography.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Representative of muscle tone, contractile force, and structural integrity; potentially related to muscle swelling or stiffness.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a half-marathon race, specifically after massage, measured at 24 hours post-race.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Assessment of muscle contractile characteristics and integrity; higher values might suggest increased damage, altered muscle properties, or impaired recovery.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Deformation time (Tc) of the muscle belly

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Not reported in this document chunk.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Measured 24 h before and after the half-marathon using Tensiomyography (TMG) as the time of muscle radial deformation between 10% and 90% Dm. Reliability: ICC = 0.90, TE = 1.86, CV = 5.8%.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicates the time and speed of muscle force generation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a half-marathon race and various recovery strategies.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Assessment of muscle contractile characteristics, indicative of fatigue and recovery.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Not reported as an effect of recovery interventions.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Samples taken during a progressive incremental field test one week prior to the half-marathon, at specified intervals and exhaustion, to determine anaerobic lactate threshold.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An indicator of anaerobic metabolism, primarily used to determine the anaerobic lactate threshold (AT).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During a pre-half-marathon incremental field test to determine anaerobic lactate threshold.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A key indicator of endurance performance, used to determine the anaerobic lactate threshold.
